Retain English Young diagrams, an $l$-multicomposition $\mu$ of $d$, its
diagram, and the row-reading initial standard tableau $t^\mu$, in which
$1,2,\dots,d$ appear in order along the successive rows from top to bottom
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]); for a single
component this is the standard tableau of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]. A $\mu$-tableau $T$ is a
placement of $1,\dots,d$ in the nodes of $\mu$. It is **row-strict** if its
entries increase from left to right in every row of every component, and
**standard** if it is row- and column-strict. The group $S_d$ acts on tableaux
by its action on entries, and for a $\mu$-tableau $T$ the permutation $w_T$ is
defined by $w_Tt^\mu=T$. The **strong Bruhat order** on tableaux is
$$S\le_BT\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_S\le w_T$$
in the Bruhat order of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], identified
with its one-based realization as in
[[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]. We write $S\unlhd T$
for $S\le_BT$ and $S\lhd T$ for strict order; the separately declared meaning
of $\unrhd$ on partitions ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) is not
reused for tableaux. On row-strict $S,T$ the order $\unlhd$ is equivalent to
the prefix-shape comparison
$$\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le a})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le a})\quad\text{for every }a,$$
where $T^{\le a}$ erases the nodes occupied by entries $>a$ and
$\operatorname{sh}$ records the resulting row lengths read in row-reading
order; this row-sequence dominance is distinct from the weak Bruhat order and
must not be reversed. The transposition criterion is
$$S=(a_1\,b_1)\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$$
with $a_n<b_n$ and $b_n$ occupying an earlier row-reading node than $a_n$ in
$(a_{n+1}\,b_{n+1})\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$ for each $n$.

For entries $r,s$ of one component define $r\to_Ts$ if they lie in the same row
and $s$ is strictly to the right of $r$; $r\downarrow_Ts$ if they lie in the
same column and $s$ is strictly below $r$; and $r\nearrow_Ts$ if $s$ is
strictly above and strictly right of $r$ (south-west is the reverse of
$\nearrow_T$). A **weak Bruhat graph edge** $T\xrightarrow{r}S$ requires both
tableaux standard, $S=s_rT$, and $r$ occupying an earlier row-reading node
than $r+1$. Equivalently $r+1\nearrow_Tr$, or $r$ lies in an earlier component
than $r+1$. In particular a same-row or same-column swap is NOT a standard
edge. A **terminal path** is a directed path in this graph, and $T$ is
$(r_1,\dots,r_m)$-**terminal** if there are standard tableaux
$S_1\xrightarrow{r_1}S_2\xrightarrow{r_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{r_m}T$.

The **Garnir belt** at a node $(a,b,n)$ with $(a+1,b,n)$ also a node of $\mu$
consists of the nodes $(a,c,n)$ for $b\le c\le\mu_a$ and the nodes
$(a+1,g,n)$ for $1\le g\le b$. The **Garnir tableau** of shape $\mu$ at
$(a,b,n)$ is the unique maximal standard $\mu$-tableau in the order $\unlhd$
among the standard $\mu$-tableaux agreeing with $t^\mu$ outside the
$(a,b,n)$-Garnir belt; it equals $t^\mu$ in the degenerate case
$b=1=\mu_a$. A **horizontal brick** is a string of consecutive entries along
same-row right arrows. For the vertical exceptional-prefix and terminal assertions assume that
$\mu$ is a multipartition; the rank, prefix-order and row-sorting assertions
allow multicompositions. The following source facts are retained with these
exact conventions and are proved below: the transposition criterion and the
prefix-shape criterion; the row-strictness of a vertical consecutive swap and
its exceptional-prefix comparison; agreement outside the Garnir belt for
tableaux below a Garnir tableau; and the four terminal alternatives for a
horizontal or vertical consecutive pair, the last alternative being $t^\mu$
for a horizontal pair and the corresponding Garnir tableau for a vertical
pair. No choice.

manifest_field_changes.before: Permutation Bruhat order is characterized by successive inversions of transpositions with the larger entry in an earlier position; placing these entries in row-reading positions gives the transposition criterion. For row-strict tableaux count the entries <=a in each row: the Bruhat rank inequalities are exactly dominance of their prefix row-count shapes, with S dominating T when w_S<=w_T. This proves the prefix criterion and its direction (the row-reading initial tableau is Bruhat-minimal and has dominant prefixes). A consecutive swap is standard exactly for strict northeast/southwest positions or different components; same-row and same-column pairs violate row/column increase. Combine this with earlier row-reading position to obtain the directed edge criterion. For a vertical consecutive swap, only prefix a=r changes; row-strictness is immediate and the exceptional-prefix comparison follows by moving its box between those two rows. Sorting each row converts the same transposition criterion to the row-strict Bruhat comparison. A tableau below a Garnir tableau can change only positions within its belt: outside row prefixes coincide, so the same rank inequalities force those entries to remain fixed. For a consecutive horizontal pair test, in order, existence of a distant terminal interchange preserving the pair, then the two adjacent terminal paths (r,r+1) and (r,r-1). If none exists, the positions r-1,...,1 and r+2,...,d are forced into row-reading order, hence T=t^mu. The identical test for a vertical pair forces exactly the maximal belt filling if none of the first three alternatives holds. This supplies the local terminal reductions used by the two-part graded-Specht induction; bricks are horizontal, not vertical chains. Actual BKW §§3.2–3.4 source proof and positional conditions checked, no finite sample computation substitutes for the general criterion. No choice.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An $l$-multicomposition $\mu$ of $d$, its row-reading initial
standard tableau $t^\mu$, the notions of row-strict and standard tableaux,
removable and addable nodes ([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]])
and partition dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) for single
components, and the one-based permutation Bruhat order with its basic
properties. We prove the finite combinatorial facts displayed in the
Definition.

[F1] For a partition, tableaux are maps from the diagram with the standard
condition and the left action of $S_n$ as declared in
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]; extending componentwise
defines $\mu$-tableaux, row-strictness, standardness and the action used here.

[F2] Dominance of partitions of $n$ is the partial order by prefix sums,
$\lambda\unrhd\nu$ for all $k$, as declared in
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]; we use the same prefix-sum comparison
on row sequences of multicompositions.

[F3] Removable and addable nodes of a partition are as declared in
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]; a node $(a,b,n)$ with
$(a+1,b,n)$ a node lets us speak of a two-row belt.

[F4] Young diagrams, their English orientation and the nodes of a
multicomposition are as declared in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

[F5] For $\sigma,\tau\in S_d$ the Bruhat order is the rank-inequality order
$r_\sigma(p,q)\ge r_\tau(p,q)$ for all $p,q$, identified with the one-based
realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$
([[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]]).

[F6] This order is the strong Bruhat order of type $A$: it is the transitive
closure of the covers $x\to tx$ with $t$ a transposition and
$\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$; it is graded by length, with every saturated chain from
$y$ to $w$ of length $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$; and $y\le w$ implies $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$
with equality only for $y=w$
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The permutation criterion.** Let $t=(a\ b)$ with $a<b$ act on values and write $p=x^{-1}(a)$, $q=x^{-1}(b)$. If $p<q$, direct inversion counting gives $\ell(tx)-\ell(x)=1+2\#\{j:p<j<q,\ a<x(j)<b\}>0$; if $p>q$ the difference is its negative. A positive difference need not equal one. The rank inequalities in [F5] show $x<tx$ precisely in the first case: the rank count decreases by one for $p\le h<q$ and $a\le k<b$, and is unchanged elsewhere. Thus every displayed earlier-node transposition lowers strong Bruhat order. Conversely a saturated strong-Bruhat chain from $w_S$ to $w_T$ consists of transposition covers by [F6], each of whose inverse lowering move has the earlier larger value by the formula just proved. Reading this chain backwards yields the displayed transposition criterion. [F5, F6, algebra]

1.2 **Agreement outside the Garnir belt.** In the row-reading initial labelling the two pieces of the belt form one contiguous interval of positions $[L,U]$: the upper-row tail is immediately followed by the lower-row prefix. A Garnir tableau changes labels only inside this interval, so $w_T$ is in the parabolic subgroup generated by $s_L,\ldots,s_{U-1}$. Sorting its interval permutation gives a reduced expression using only these generators. The Bruhat subword criterion applied to this expression says that every $w_S\le w_T$ likewise uses only these generators. Hence $w_S$ fixes all positions outside $[L,U]$, proving agreement with $t^\mu$ outside the belt. This applies even to nonstandard $S$. [F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 **The prefix-shape criterion.** For a row-strict $W$ and a value $c$, row-strictness makes the entries $\le c$ in each row a prefix, so $\operatorname{sh}(W^{\le c})$ is a row sequence of size $c$, and for $p=P_k+t$ with $P_k$ the number of nodes in the first $k$ rows and $0\le t<\mu_{k+1}$ we get $$N_W(p,c):=\#\{i\le p:\text{entry }i\text{ of }W\le c\}=A_k(W,c)+\min\bigl(t,s_{k+1}(W,c)\bigr),$$ where $A_k(W,c)$ is the number of entries $\le c$ in the first $k$ rows and $s_{k+1}(W,c)$ the prefix length in row $k+1$. By [F5], $w_S\le w_T$ iff $N_S(p,c)\ge N_T(p,c)$ for all $p,c$. At $p=P_k$ this says $A_k(S,c)\ge A_k(T,c)$ for all $k,c$, which is exactly $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le c})$ for all $c$; hence the prefix criterion is necessary. Conversely assume all these prefix inequalities, fix $p=P_k+t$ and put $a=A_k(S,c)-A_k(T,c)\ge0$, $s=s_{k+1}(S,c)$, $s'=s_{k+1}(T,c)$; the inequality at $k+1$ gives $a+s\ge s'$. If $t\le s$ then $a+\min(t,s)=a+t\ge\min(t,s')$, because $t\le s'$ gives $a+t\ge t$ and $t>s'$ gives $a+t\ge t\ge s'$; if $t>s$ then $a+\min(t,s)=a+s\ge s'\ge\min(t,s')$. Thus $N_S(p,c)\ge N_T(p,c)$ for all $p,c$ and $S\unlhd T$. Since the first $k$ rows of $t^\mu$ contain $\min(c,P_k)$ entries $\le c$, the maximum possible, $\operatorname{sh}(t^{\mu\le c})$ dominates every $\operatorname{sh}(W^{\le c})$, so $t^\mu$ is the least element of $\unlhd$ on row-strict tableaux. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, F2]

3.1 **Consecutive swaps and the edges of the weak graph.** Let $T$ be standard. If $r,r+1$ share a row, row-strictness puts $r$ immediately left of $r+1$ and the swap reverses an adjacent pair, so $s_rT$ is not row-strict; if they share a column, column-strictness puts $r$ immediately above $r+1$ and the swap reverses an adjacent column pair, so $s_rT$ is not column-strict. If in one component $r+1$ lies strictly above and strictly left of $r$, let $x$ be the entry of $T$ in the node in the row of $r$ and the column of $r+1$: row-strictness gives $x<r$ while column-strictness gives $x>r+1$, impossible, and symmetrically $r$ cannot lie strictly above and strictly left of $r+1$. The only remaining same-component configurations are $r\nearrow_Tr+1$ and $r+1\nearrow_Tr$; in either, the nodes sharing a row or column with the two positions are unchanged except for the interchange of the consecutive values $r,r+1$, so all strict neighbour inequalities survive and $s_rT$ is standard. If $r,r+1$ lie in different components the swap is standard as well. This proves the stated equivalence. For the edge criterion note that $S=s_rT$ with both standard and $r$ earlier than $r+1$ in $T$: in one component the alternatives of the equivalence leave only $r+1\nearrow_Tr$ (in the other alternative $r+1$ is in a higher row and hence earlier, and same-row or same-column swaps are excluded), while in different components $r$ is earlier exactly when its component is earlier. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 **Row sorting.** Let $S,T$ be $\mu$-tableaux with $S\unlhd T$; by steps 1.1 and 2.1 it suffices to treat a single transposition $S=(a\,b)T$ with $a<b$ and $b$ earlier than $a$ in $T$, the general case following by composing the finitely many single-swap comparisons. Write $S^+,T^+$ for the tableaux obtained by sorting every row increasingly. If $a,b$ share a row of $T$, then $S$ and $T$ have the same row sets and $S^+=T^+$. Otherwise the node of $b$ lies in a strictly earlier row than the node of $a$: they are in different rows by the previous sentence, and $b$ earlier than $a$ forces $b$'s row to be the earlier one. Entries other than $a,b$ occupy the same nodes in $S$ and $T$. For a value $c$, the prefix row lengths of $S^+$ and $T^+$ at $c$ are the rows' counts of entries $\le c$; if $c<a$ or $c\ge b$ these counts agree, while if $a\le c<b$ the count vector of $S^+$ is obtained from that of $T^+$ by moving one unit from the row of $a$ to the earlier row of $b$. Moving a unit to an earlier row raises every partial sum of the row sequence, so $\operatorname{sh}(S^{+\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{+\le c})$ for every $c$; both tableaux are row-strict, so step 2.1 gives $S^+\unlhd T^+$. Hence $S\unlhd T$ implies $S^+\unlhd T^+$ in general. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]



4.1 **The vertical consecutive swap and its exceptional prefix.** Assume $\mu$ is a multipartition, $T$ standard, $r\downarrow_Tr+1$, so $r$ and $r+1$ occupy adjacent rows $a,a+1$ of one component in the same column $b$; the neighbour check of step 3.1 shows that $U:=s_rT$ is row-strict. Let $S$ be standard with $S\lhd U$; we prove $S\unlhd T$. By step 2.1, $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le c})$ for all $c$, and for $c\ne r$ the tableaux $U^{\le c}$ and $T^{\le c}$ occupy the same nodes, so their shapes agree. For $c=r$ let $A_k$ be the number of entries $\le r-1$ in the first $k$ rows of $T$ (the same for $U$) and note that $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$ has row lengths $A_k-A_{k-1}+[k=a+1]$ while $\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$ has $A_k-A_{k-1}+[k=a]$; thus $\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$ is obtained from $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$ by moving one node from row $a+1$ up to row $a$. Because $T$ is standard, the node of $r$ in row $a$ has column $b$, so exactly $b-1$ entries of row $a$ lie in columns $<b$, all of them $\le r-1$, and the same count holds in row $a+1$ whose node in column $b$ is occupied by $r+1$; hence $A_a-A_{a-1}=b-1=A_{a+1}-A_a$ and the switch hypothesis $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})_a-\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})_{a+1}=(b-1)-((b-1)+1)=-1$ holds. Lemma 3.1 of the source, proved here: if $\nu$ is a row sequence and $\nu_a-\nu_{a+1}=-1$, and $\hat\nu$ interchanges the two consecutive parts $\nu_a,\nu_{a+1}$, then $\hat\nu$ has the same partial sums as $\nu$ except at index $a$, where they are larger by one; consequently any multipartition $\lambda$ with $\lambda\unrhd\nu$ also satisfies $\lambda\unrhd\hat\nu$: if its partial sum at $a$ equalled that of $\nu$, the inequalities at $a-1$ and $a+1$ would force $\lambda_a\le\nu_a<\nu_{a+1}\le\lambda_{a+1}$, contradicting the weakly decreasing parts in that component. Thus its partial sum at $a$ is at least one larger; other partial sums are unchanged. Apply this with $\lambda=\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le r})$, $\nu=\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$, $\hat\nu=\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$: the row sequence of a standard tableau's prefix is a multipartition, and the computed switch identity verifies the hypothesis, so $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le r})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$. With the equalities for $c\ne r$, step 2.1 gives $S\unlhd T$. In the same-row case $r\to_Tr+1$ one has $T=U^+$ and $S=S^+$, so step 3.2 gives $S\unlhd T$ directly; this proves both clauses of the vertical exceptional-prefix fact. [step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra]

4.2 **The four terminal alternatives (horizontal).** Let $\mu$ be a multipartition and $T$ be standard with $r\to_Tr+1$. Consider the three properties: (a) there is $t$ with $|t-r|>1$ such that $t\nearrow_Tt+1$ or $t$ lies in a later component than $t+1$; (b) $r+1\nearrow_Tr+2$ or $r+1$ lies in a later component than $r+2$; (c) $r-1\nearrow_Tr$ or $r-1$ lies in a later component than $r$. By step 3.1 an incoming edge at $t$ (that is, $s_tT$ standard with $t$ earlier than $t+1$ in $s_tT$) is equivalent to $t\nearrow_Tt+1$ or $t$ in a later component than $t+1$. If (a) holds, then $X:=s_tT$ is standard and $X\xrightarrow{t}T$ is an edge, so $T$ is $t$-terminal, and since $t\notin\{r,r+1\}$ the relation $r\to_Tr+1$ persists in $X$; this is alternative (1). If (b) holds with $r+1\nearrow_Tr+2$, then in $X:=s_{r+1}T$ the entry $r+1$ occupies the higher node of $r+2$, so $X\xrightarrow{r+1}T$ is an edge; since $r,r+1$ are adjacent in one row and $r+2$ is above and right, $r+1$ is above and right of $r$ in $X$, so $Y:=s_rX$ is standard and $Y\xrightarrow{r}X$ is an edge with $r$ moving to the higher node, and in $Y$ the entries $r+1,r+2$ are adjacent in one row with $r+1$ to the left; this is alternative (2). If (b) holds with $r+1$ in a later component than $r+2$, the same construction with component arguments gives (2). If (c) holds, the mirror construction gives (3). It remains to observe that if none of (a),(b),(c) holds, then $T$ has no incoming edge: indeed (a) is exactly the incoming-edge alternative at any $t\notin\{r-1,r,r+1\}$, (c) at $t=r-1$, and (b) at $t=r+1$, while at $t=r$ both alternatives of step 3.1 fail because $r$ and $r+1$ lie in one row with $r$ to the left. A standard tableau with no incoming edge is $t^\mu$: if $T\ne t^\mu$, choose the least $t$ with the node of $t+1$ earlier than the node of $t$ in $T$ (such $t$ exists because otherwise the entries occur in the order $1,2,\dots,d$); then standardness forces $t\nearrow_Tt+1$ or an earlier component for $t+1$, so the incoming-edge alternative at $t$ holds and gives the existence of an edge into $T$, a contradiction. Hence in this final case $T=t^\mu$, which is alternative (4). [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **The vertical terminal alternatives.** Let $\mu$ be a multipartition and $r\downarrow_Tr+1$ at $(a,b,n)$, so the two nodes are vertically adjacent. Use the following precise tests: (a) an incoming edge $t$ with $|t-r|>1$; (b) $r\nearrow_Tr+2$ or $r+1$ is in a later component than $r+2$; (c) $r-1\nearrow_Tr+1$ or $r-1$ is in a later component than $r$. Test (a) gives $s_tT\xrightarrow{t}T$ and preserves the vertical pair. In test (b), standardness and the consecutiveness of the three entries force $s_{r+1}T$ and $s_rs_{r+1}T$ to be standard: the node of $r+2$ is above and right of $r$, hence above and right of the node of $r+1$, and after the first swap the nodes of $r,r+1$ are incomparable. Thus $s_rs_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r+1}T$, while $r+1,r+2$ occupy the original vertical pair in $s_rs_{r+1}T$. The different-component case uses the same two swaps without any within-component inequality. Test (c) gives the analogous $s_rs_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r-1}T$, with $r-1,r$ in the original vertical pair. If none of the tests holds, labels other than the triple adjacent to $r$ cannot have an inversion between consecutive row-reading positions: any such inverse-order consecutive pair is in incomparable nodes or distinct components and is exactly an incoming edge. Reading $r-1,r-2,\ldots,1$ backwards and $r+2,r+3,\ldots,d$ forwards consequently places them in row-reading order except for the lower-row prefix before the vertical pair and the upper-row tail after it; tests (c) and (b) exclude any further excursion. More explicitly, if $L$ is the initial label at $(a,b,n)$ and $U$ the initial label at $(a+1,b,n)$, the forced belt filling is $L,\ldots,L+b-2$ in the first $b-1$ lower-row positions, $r=L+b-1$ in $(a,b,n)$, $r+1=L+b$ in $(a+1,b,n)$, and $L+b+1,\ldots,U$ in the remaining upper-row tail; all outside entries are unchanged. Among standard belt fillings this is Bruhat-maximal: the $b$ lower-row entries are the lexicographically smallest possible increasing subset, namely $L,\ldots,L+b-2,L+b$, because choosing the $b$ smallest would violate column $b$. Every other valid subset has no smaller prefix counts in the upper row, hence is below it by step 2.1. This is exactly the Garnir tableau, including $b=1=\mu_a$. A horizontal brick is a consecutive same-row string. All selections, chains and comparisons are finite, so no choice principle is used. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

function $\deg(T)$.

[F1] The module $S(\mu)$, the elements $z_T$, $v_T$ and the degree recursion
are those of

cellularity and ordinary dominance-raising Garnir straightening are
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]] and
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]].

[F2] The weak Bruhat graph, the triangularity of the tableau order and the
Garnir/terminal alternatives are those of
[[def-tableau-domination-order-garnir-tableaux-and-bricks]]; standard tableaux
and reduced words for $w_T$ are those of

lemma, are those of [[lem-degree-and-codegree-of-standard-tableaux]]; the

[[prop-shifted-degrees-and-garnir-exchanges-for-standard-tableaux]].

[F4] The KLR presentation, its grading and the degrees $\deg e(i)=0$,
$\deg y_r=2$, $\deg\psi_re(i)=-a_{i_ri_{r+1}}$ are those of

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Ungraded straightening and triangularity.** The cellular Murphy straightening in [F1], in its left version, expresses $z_U$ for any tableau $U$ as a sum of standard $z_S$ with $w_S\le w_U$; row sorting is passage to the parabolic minimal representative, hence lowers Bruhat order; each Garnir replacement raises prefix dominance, hence strictly lowers Bruhat order by the row-boundary rank-count equivalence proved in [F2]. The standard $z_T=m_{T,t^\mu}+K(\mu)$ are independent because they are distinct surviving cellular basis elements, and they span the cyclic module by that straightening. The initial-vector calculation in the Definition gives $e(i_{t^\mu})z_\mu=z_\mu$ and $y_az_\mu=0$. In the fixed BK presentation, $\psi_re(i)=(T_r+P_r(i))Q_r(i)^{-1}e(i)$, where $Q_r(i)$ has invertible constant term. Expand a reduced product and slide dots right using the mixed relations: the result is a sum $T_{r_{a_1}}\cdots T_{r_{a_b}}f(y)z_\mu$ over subwords, and the full-subword coefficient is a product of nonzero constants $Q_r(i)^{-1}(0)$. Rightmost dots evaluate at zero. The Hecke quadratic relation and the Bruhat subword criterion reduce each proper subword to $T_uz_\mu$ with $u<w_T$, so Murphy straightening gives $v_T=a_Tz_T+\sum_{S\lhd T}a_Sz_S$, with $a_T\ne0$ for standard $T$. This proves a basis for each selected reduced-word family and also straightens every nonstandard $v_U$ into standard $v_S$ with $S\unlhd U$. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 **Filtered KLR word calculus before a grading on the module.** A dot moved through a crossing becomes the permuted dot plus a scalar term only for equal residues; moving all dots to the right thus deletes crossings in every scalar error. Two reduced words are connected by Coxeter moves. A distant move is exact; a length-three braid changes the product to a polynomial in dots times the remaining word, deleting the three crossings of that braid. A nonreduced word is shortened by bringing a repeated simple reflection together through these moves and replacing its square by its KLR quadratic polynomial. Induction on word length, using the deletion/subword criterion, therefore writes every error as $\psi_uf(y)e(i_{t^\mu})$ with $u<w_T$ and preserves its algebra degree. Acting on $z_\mu$ kills positive-degree rightmost dot monomials. Combined with step 1.1 this gives, without presupposing module homogeneity: reduced-word changes have only $v_S$ with $S\lhd T$; $y_av_T$ has only $S\lhd T$; and if $a,a+1$ share a row or column, $\psi_av_T$ has only $S\lhd T$ and $i_S=s_ai_T$. For the last assertion first straighten below $s_aT$ and use the exceptional-prefix comparison of [F2] to get $S\unlhd T$; equality is excluded because adjacent same-row or same-column boxes have distinct residues for $e\ge2$. Weight support follows directly from $\psi_ae(i)=e(s_ai)\psi_a$ and commuting dots. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **The simultaneous induction.** Assign degree $\deg T$ to the selected basis $v_T$. Prove together, for $m\ge0$, (a) word-change errors at standard tableaux of length at most $m$ have degree $\deg T$, and (b) all dot and crossing actions at standard tableaux of length at most $m-1$ have their prescribed degrees. The base $m=0$ has the unique length-zero tableau $t^\mu$ and no action assertion. For (a), a nontrivial braid error has at most $m-3$ crossings after step 2.1 and the same algebra degree as the original reduced word. Act on $z_\mu$ successively with the at most $m-3$ crossings of each shortened term, expanding after each action in the ungraded selected standard basis. Step 1.1 bounds every appearing standard-tableau length by the number of crossings so far, and step 2.1 gives the corresponding bound after straightening a nonreduced product. Thus before every action the standard-basis lengths are at most $m-4$, and the already proved action assertion (b) applies. No standardness of an arbitrary subword tableau is assumed. By [F3] the algebra degree plus $\deg(t^\mu)$ is $\deg T$. Strict-order straightening and weight support in step 2.1 therefore give exactly the difference formula (2). A sequence of braid moves gives it for any two words. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **Dot actions in the induction.** At $\ell(T)=m-1$ write $v_T=\psi_av_U$ with $\ell(U)=m-2$; word changes only add shorter vectors of the same degree by step 3.1. Slide $y_r$ past $\psi_a$. The main term is $\psi_ay_{s_a(r)}v_U$, and the possible scalar error is $\pm v_U$ at equal crossing colors. The dot action at $U$ is homogeneous by induction and, by step 2.1, is supported on lengths strictly below $m-2$, so applying $\psi_a$ to all its basis terms is covered by induction. The mixed relation is homogeneous, so both the main term and the scalar error have degree $\deg T+2$. When $T=t^\mu$, the dot is zero. This proves every dot assertion at length $m-1$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Crossing actions at standard swaps.** If $s_rT$ is standard and has length $m$, the word $s_rw_T$ is reduced, so the word-change assertion just proved at length $m$ and the weak-edge identity in [F3] give degree $\deg T-a_{i_ri_{r+1}}$. If $s_rT$ instead has length $m-2$, write $v_T=\psi_rv_{s_rT}$ up to shorter same-weight same-degree errors. Apply $\psi_r$: the main term becomes $Q_{i_ri_{r+1}}(y_r,y_{r+1})v_{s_rT}$, and the other terms are crossing actions at strictly shorter tableaux. Those actions are covered by induction and the dot polynomial by step 4.1 and induction. Homogeneity of the quadratic relation gives the required degree also for this case. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 **Crossing actions at a horizontal or vertical pair.** The four terminal alternatives of [F2] complete the crossing induction. For a distant terminal edge $t$, write $v_T=\psi_tv_U$ up to shorter homogeneous errors, with $|t-r|>1$. Commute $\psi_r$ past $\psi_t$. The action $\psi_rv_U$ is supported strictly below $U$ by step 2.1 because the horizontal or vertical relation persists, so both successive actions are already covered by induction and their degree is the homogeneous product degree. For a two-edge terminal alternative write $v_T=\psi_{r\pm1}\psi_rv_U$ up to shorter homogeneous errors, where $\ell(U)=m-3$ and $r\pm1,r\pm1+1$ are horizontal or vertical in $U$. The braid relation rewrites $\psi_r\psi_{r\pm1}\psi_rv_U$ as $\psi_{r\pm1}\psi_r\psi_{r\pm1}v_U$ plus the homogeneous dot correction. By step 2.1 the first action on the rewritten word is supported strictly below $U$, so all remaining actions use strictly shorter lengths and induction; step 4.1 handles the dot correction. The horizontal terminal base is $T=t^\mu$: step 2.1 makes $\psi_rv_T=0$. The vertical terminal base is the Garnir tableau. Here step 2.1 gives only $v_S$ with $S\lhd T$ and $i_S=s_ri_T$, and the Garnir exchange formula in [F3] gives $\deg S=\deg T-a_{i_ri_{r+1}}$ for every such term. This proves (b), completing the simultaneous induction without assuming the homogeneity being proved. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 **Grading, character and independence.** The weight identity in step 2.1 and the action degrees established in steps 4.1–6.1 show that the vector-space grading is a module grading. Zero images belong to the stated homogeneous components; a degree is asserted only for a nonzero vector. Step 3.1 makes every change of selected reduced words a unitriangular basis change within each weight and degree, so it preserves the graded subspaces while individual $v_T$ may change. Finally the homogeneous basis yields $\operatorname{ch}_qS(\mu)=\sum_Tq^{\deg T}i_T$ and the construction used exactly the original ungraded left Murphy cell. Every selection is finite and requires no choice principle. [F1, F4, step 3.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

$d^A$ is the number of addable $i$-nodes strictly above $A$ minus the number of
removable $i$-nodes strictly above $A$, computed in $\mu\setminus A$
([[lem-standard-fock-vectors-expand-in-the-upper-global-basis]]).

[F3] The integral highest weight module $V_A(\Lambda_0)$ and its dual are
irreducible over $\mathbb Q(q)$, with generated highest-weight submodules
determined by the highest vector
([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]); the normalized contravariant form satisfies
$B(F_ix,y)=B(x,q^{-1}K_iE_iy)$
([[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]); the
transported identification $\Psi_{\rm can}^{\rm Hecke}$ intertwines the
canonical $E_i$ with the Fock node action
([[prop-qg8-categorification-transports-across-the-hecke-klr-bridge]],
[[thm-cyclotomic-klr-functors-define-an-integrable-quantum-action-on-k-zero-and-g-zero]]).

[F4] The degree identities $d_A(\mu)+d^A(\mu\setminus A)=h_i(\alpha)+1$ and
$d_i(\mu)=(\Lambda_0-\alpha,\alpha_i)$ are the content of
[[lem-degree-and-codegree-of-standard-tableaux]] in the level-one convention.

[C1] Choice is inherited only through the declared global-basis interfaces
used to identify the integral dual lattice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[prop-qg8-categorification-transports-across-the-hecke-klr-bridge]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Evaluate on projective words.** For a residue word $\mathbf i=(i_1,\ldots,i_d)$ of content $\alpha$, put $P(\mathbf i)=R^\Lambda_\alpha e(\mathbf i)$ and transport it to the Hecke block. Appending the strands successively realizes it as $F_{i_d}^{\rm basic}\cdots F_{i_1}^{\rm basic}$ of the vacuum projective, so [F1] sends its class to $F_{i_d}\cdots F_{i_1}v_{\Lambda_0}$. The generator-fixing anti-involution identifies $P(\mathbf i)^\psi$ with the right ideal $e(\mathbf i)R^\Lambda_\alpha$, and multiplication gives $e(\mathbf i)R^\Lambda_\alpha\otimes_{R^\Lambda_\alpha}S(\mu)\cong e(\mathbf i)S(\mu)$. Thus the defining bilinear tensor pairing, without any Hom-pairing bar on a shifted first argument, gives $\Psi_{\rm can}^{\rm Hecke}([S(\mu)])(F_{i_d}\cdots F_{i_1}v_{\Lambda_0})=\sum_{T:i_T=\mathbf i}q^{\deg T}$. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 **The identical standard-coordinate evaluation.** If $A$ is a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ and $\alpha=\operatorname{cont}(\mu)$, the Fock formula [F2] gives its removal coefficient $q^{-d^A(\mu\setminus A)}$. The operator $K_i$ on the resulting weight $\Lambda_0-\alpha+\alpha_i$ multiplies by $q^{h_i(\alpha)+2}$. Contravariance of [F3] therefore gives the coefficient of $M_\mu$ in $F_iM_{\mu\setminus A}$ as $q^{h_i(\alpha)+1-d^A(\mu\setminus A)}=q^{d_A(\mu)}$, by [F4]. Iterating additions from the vacuum enumerates precisely the standard tableaux of shape $\mu$ with successive residues $\mathbf i$: at each stage the occupied nodes form a partition, and conversely its increasing filling records the addition path. The product of the node factors is $q^{\sum_A d_A}=q^{\deg T}$ by the degree recursion. Hence the coordinate functional $\operatorname{Std}_\mu(x)=B(x,M_\mu)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Std}_\mu(F_{i_d}\cdots F_{i_1}v_{\Lambda_0})=\sum_{T:i_T=\mathbf i}q^{\deg T}$, exactly step 1.1. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 **Equality in the restricted integral dual.** The basic highest-weight module over $\mathbb Q(q)$ is generated from the vacuum by the negative generators, so its vectors $F_{i_d}\cdots F_{i_1}v_{\Lambda_0}$ span every weight space; no assertion that ordinary words alone span the divided-power lattice over $A$ is needed. Steps 1.1–2.1 make the two functionals equal on this field spanning family. Both lie in the restricted integral weight dual by [F1] and the coordinate-functional construction of [F2]; their field equality therefore is equality in that lattice. Under the nondegenerate contravariant form, $\operatorname{Std}_\mu$ is represented by $S_\mu=\pi(M_\mu)$, giving the stated equation. It holds in both field-characteristic branches because the homogeneous basis and integral categorical pairing do, and uses no cellular head classification or characteristic-zero based theorem. Choice is precisely the inherited [C1]. [C1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A partition $\mu$ of $d$ with content $\alpha$, a residue $i$, the
removable $i$-nodes $A_1,\dots,A_c$ ordered bottom to top, and the graded
Specht module $S(\mu)$ with its homogeneous tableau basis.

[F1] The graded Specht module $S(\mu)$, its degree recursion and the standard
vectors $v_T$ are those of
[[def-graded-specht-module-by-homogeneous-standard-tableaux]]; by
[[thm-graded-specht-module-has-homogeneous-tableau-basis]] the $v_T$ form a
homogeneous basis with $v_T\in e(i_T)S(\mu)$ and
$\deg(y_rv_T)=\deg(y_r)+\deg(T)$,
$\deg(\psi_rv_T)=\deg(\psi_re(i_T))+\deg(T)$.

[F2] The restriction functor $E_i$, the idempotent decomposition
$\operatorname{Res}=\bigoplus_iE_i$ and the tower induction/restriction
bimodules are those of
[[def-cyclotomic-klr-induction-and-restriction-functors]] and
[[def-klr-induction-and-restriction-bimodules]]; the type-$A$ specialization
and its Cartan data are those of
[[def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras]].

[F3] Tableaux, the weak Bruhat arrows and the removable/addable node
conventions, in particular the bottom-to-top order of removable nodes, are
those of [[def-tableau-domination-order-garnir-tableaux-and-bricks]]; the
shifted-degree and Garnir-exchange formulas are those of
[[prop-shifted-degrees-and-garnir-exchanges-for-standard-tableaux]].

[F4] Over $\mathcal R=\mathbb Z[u,u^{-1}]$ the left Murphy cell has the
free standard basis $z_T=T_{w_T}z_\mu$ and is compatible with every base
change ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Over its fraction
field $\mathcal K=\mathbb Q(u)$ the cell-level JM eigenbasis has
$f_T=z_T+\sum_{S\lhd T}b_Sz_S$. Its adjacent-generator coefficients are
$u$ on a row, $-1$ on a column, and on a standard swap are the two
seminormal coefficients of
[[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]],
clauses (2)–(4). These depend only on the two node contents and the relative
tableau dominance. We use its individual-cell diagonalization and generator
formulas, not a global JM label theorem or a finite-$e$ simple classification.
The right-cell formulas convert to left formulas by star, which fixes $T_r$
and the additive JM elements.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The ordered Murphy subspaces over the universal ring.** First work with the ungraded level-one left Murphy cell $S_{\mathcal R}(\mu)$ at the universal Hecke parameter $u$, where $\mathcal R=\mathbb Z[u,u^{-1}]$. List all removable corners as $B_1,\ldots,B_b$ from bottom to top. Define $W_j^{\mathcal R}$ to be the span of standard $z_T$ with the maximal entry $d$ in $B_1,\ldots,B_j$. Each is a free basis-coordinate subspace, with free quotient. If $S\unlhd T$ in the tableau Bruhat order, its prefix of size $d-1$ dominates the corresponding prefix of $T$ by [F3]. For corners of a fixed partition, $\mu\setminus B$ dominates $\mu\setminus A$ exactly when $B$ is lower than or equal to $A$: subtracting a node from a lower row retains one extra node in every intervening upper-row prefix sum. Thus every standard tableau below $T$ has $d$ in the same or a lower corner. This is the direction needed for the bottom-to-top filtration. [F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 **Prove stability generically and descend exact coefficients.** Extend scalars to $\mathcal K=\mathbb Q(u)$ and use the cell-level triangular eigenbasis of [F4]. Step 1.1 implies $W_j^{\mathcal K}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathcal K}\{f_T:d\text{ in }B_1,\ldots,B_j\}$: the triangular basis change and its inverse preserve each such set. For $1\le r<d-1$, the seminormal formula for $T_r f_T$ involves only $f_T$ and, when standard, $f_{s_rT}$. Both have $d$ in the same node, so every $W_j^{\mathcal K}$ is an $H_{\mathcal K,u}(S_{d-1})$-submodule. The action matrix of $T_r$ on the universal $z$-basis has coefficients in $\mathcal R$ by [F4]. Every coefficient exiting $W_j^{\mathcal R}$ vanishes after the injective extension $\mathcal R\hookrightarrow\mathcal K$, hence is zero already in $\mathcal R$. Therefore $W_j^{\mathcal R}$ is a submodule. This proves only stability of the ordered sums; it makes no claim that individual fixed-corner spans are stable after specialization. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **Identify the generic corner quotient on its standard vectors.** Fix $j$, put $A=B_j$ and $\nu=\mu\setminus A$, and let $T_A$ be the standard filling with $d$ in $A$ and the remaining entries row-filled in $\nu$. For any standard $T$ with $d$ in $A$, deletion gives $\bar T$ of shape $\nu$. On the eigenbasis quotient $W_j^{\mathcal K}/W_{j-1}^{\mathcal K}$ the map $f_T\mapsto f_{\bar T}$ is an $H_{d-1}$-isomorphism: for every generator $T_r$, $r<d-1$, the two contents, same-row/column alternatives, standardness of the swap and relative prefix dominance are unchanged by deleting $d$; hence the two displayed seminormal action matrices in [F4] are identical. The tableau $T_A$ is dominance-maximal among tableaux with $d$ in $A$, since its deleted tableau is row-filled. Thus the triangular correction to $f_{T_A}$ has only tableaux with $d$ in lower corners, so $f_{T_A}+W_{j-1}^{\mathcal K}=z_{T_A}+W_{j-1}^{\mathcal K}$. The initial eigenvector of $S_{\mathcal K}(\nu)$ is $f_{t^\nu}=z_\nu$. If the row-reading index of $A$ in $\mu$ is $k$, the permutation $w_{T_A}$ sends the initial entry $k$ to $d$ and shifts $k+1,\ldots,d$ down by one, and has length $d-k$. The factorization $w_T=w_{\bar T}w_{T_A}$ is length-additive: the $d-k$ inversions involving $d$ are fixed, and all other inversions are precisely those of $w_{\bar T}$. Therefore $z_T=T_{w_{\bar T}}z_{T_A}$, and the generic isomorphism sends $z_T+W_{j-1}^{\mathcal K}$ exactly to $z_{\bar T}$. This identifies the standardized quotient map, not just an unspecified generic module isomorphism. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **The integral and specialized deletion quotient.** Define the $\mathcal R$-linear basis map $W_j^{\mathcal R}/W_{j-1}^{\mathcal R}\to S_{\mathcal R}(\nu)$ by $z_T\mapsto z_{\bar T}$. Both source and target are free with these corresponding bases. For each finite Hecke generator, both action matrices have entries in $\mathcal R$, and step 3.1 makes their difference zero in $\mathcal K$. Injectivity of $\mathcal R\to\mathcal K$ therefore makes that difference zero over $\mathcal R$. This is an integral module isomorphism. Base change $u\mapsto\xi$ gives the exact Murphy restriction filtration and deletion quotients over the original field $F$, including singular finite-$e$ parameters and positive characteristic. Because every inclusion was a basis-coordinate inclusion with free quotient, these scalar extensions preserve the entire filtration and its quotients; no flatness assumption on $F$ is needed and no generic denominator is specialized. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Pass to the selected homogeneous basis and establish the shift.** Return to the fixed graded Hecke–KLR presentation. Its homogeneous theorem [F1] gives a triangular change $v_T=a_Tz_T+\sum_{S\lhd T}a_Sz_S$, $a_T\ne0$. Step 1.1 therefore identifies every specialized $W_j$ with the span of the selected $v_T$ having $d$ in $B_1,\ldots,B_j$, so $W_j$ is a graded submodule. To verify that the deletion isomorphism of step 4.1 is homogeneous, choose compatible reduced words $w_T=w_{\bar T}w_{T_A}$, which are reduced by step 3.1. The grading is independent of this selected-word change by [F1]. The triangular expansion of $v_{T_A}$ has only lower-corner terms besides its nonzero leading term, so its image under the ungraded deletion quotient is $a_Az_\nu$ for a fixed scalar $a_A\ne0$. The previous-rank generators have the same tower images under the transported KLR presentation: the inclusion keeps $X_r,T_r$ for $r<d$; hence its weight idempotent $e(\mathbf i)$ becomes $\sum_j e(\mathbf i,j)$, since both project onto the generalized eigenspaces of those same first $d-1$ commuting $X$ operators. The defining dot formula and fixed crossing normalizing series use only the same adjacent $X$ operators, so $y_r$ for $r\le d-1$ and $\psi_r$ for $r<d-1$ are unchanged. This is the tower transport in [F2], without assigning any simple-module shape from a JM tuple; consequently the deletion map sends $v_T+W_{j-1}=\psi_{w_{\bar T}}v_{T_A}+W_{j-1}$ to $a_Av_{\bar T}$. Rescaling the quotient map by $a_A^{-1}$ gives the homogeneous-basis correspondence. The degree recursion [F1] gives $\deg T=\deg\bar T+d_A(\mu)$, so $W_j/W_{j-1}\cong S(\nu)\{d_A(\mu)\}$ as graded modules. Other preferred words preserve the same graded subspaces and graded isomorphism by [F1]; no word-independence of the individual vectors is asserted. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 **Select the removable-$i$-node filtration.** The residue projector $e(\alpha-\alpha_i,\alpha_i)$ on restriction selects exactly the homogeneous basis vectors whose last residue is $i$ by [F1, F2]. Apply this exact idempotent summand to the all-corner filtration of step 5.1. A quotient for a corner $B_j$ of residue different from $i$ becomes zero, while a quotient for an $i$-corner remains $S(\mu\setminus B_j)\{d_{B_j}(\mu)\}$. Removing the repeated zero steps leaves precisely the bottom-to-top sequence $A_1,\ldots,A_c$ of the Statement, with $V_m$ spanned by the selected $v_T$ whose last node is among $A_1,\ldots,A_m$. This proves the asserted filtration and all graded quotients. If there are no removable $i$-nodes the selected module is zero and the filtration is empty; rank zero has no restriction assertion. The entire argument uses finite bases, finite spectra and explicit scalar extension, so no choice principle or cellular head classification is used. [F1, F2, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nondegenerate level-one regime in either field branch, its
finite-dimensional graded block $B=R^\Lambda_\alpha$ (or the transported Hecke
block), the graded left Murphy cells $S(\mu)$ and dominance order.

[F1] The ungraded cells are the Murphy cells, their form quotients are
absolutely simple exactly at the restricted labels, and these quotients exhaust
the ungraded simples over every stated field
([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]).
Every proper submodule of a nonzero-form cell lies in its form radical;
$[S(\mu):D_\lambda]\ne0$ forces $\lambda\unlhd\mu$, and
$[S(\lambda):D_\lambda]=1$
([[lem-finite-cellular-nonzero-form-heads-purity-and-shared-factor-linkage]]).
The left version is obtained through cellular star.

[F2] The homogeneous tableau basis supplies precisely the grading on these
same ungraded cells
([[thm-graded-specht-module-has-homogeneous-tableau-basis]],
[[def-graded-specht-module-by-homogeneous-standard-tableaux]]).
The restricted labels and order are
[[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]] and
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]].

[F3] In both branches the canonical restricted-dual identification sends
$[S(\mu)]$ to the standard coordinate functional $\operatorname{Std}_\mu$
([[thm-graded-specht-classes-realize-standard-fock-vectors]]).
The restricted coordinate functionals form an $A$-basis and satisfy
$\operatorname{Std}_\mu=\sum_\nu d_{(\nu,\mu)}(q)G^*(\nu)$ with dominance support
and restricted diagonal $1$
([[lem-standard-fock-vectors-expand-in-the-upper-global-basis]],
[[def-level-one-global-basis-transition-polynomials-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]).
Here the upper bar is the adjoint of lower bar and fixes $G^*(\nu)$.

[F4] In (C0) only, the crystal-labelled normalized simple classes are the
upper global vectors and their multiplicities are $d_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q)$
([[thm-ariki-canonical-basis-theorem-in-characteristic-zero]],
[[thm-graded-decomposition-numbers-equal-canonical-basis-coefficients-in-characteristic-zero]],
[[prop-qg8-categorification-transports-across-the-hecke-klr-bridge]]).

[F5] The ordinary signed-conjugate module and unit-scaled form dictionary are
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]],
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]] and
[[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]].

[F6] In both branches each graded simple shift orbit has a unique
$D_\psi$-self-dual representative, independently of any characteristic-zero
global-basis theorem
([[lem-cyclotomic-projective-covers-and-dualities-descend-through-the-quotient]],
[[def-cyclotomic-klr-diagram-duality-and-graded-module-duals]]).
On the Hecke side the transported anti-involution is
$\rho\psi\rho^{-1}$; it is not identified with raw Murphy star
([[lem-graded-algebra-isomorphism-transports-the-graded-module-category]]).
Write $\circledast=D_\psi$ and use the shifts of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

[F7] The projective map sends the word projective $Be(\mathbf i)$ to the
corresponding negative-generator word on the vacuum; these words span the
highest-weight module over $\mathbb Q(q)$. The module map is defined by
$\Psi(M)(\phi(P))=T(P,M)$, where $T$ is the bilinear tensor pairing and
$h(P,M)=T(P^\#,M)$ is the first-bar-sesquilinear Hom pairing
([[thm-cyclotomic-klr-projective-k-zero-is-the-integral-highest-weight-module]],
[[thm-cyclotomic-klr-module-g-zero-is-the-dual-integral-highest-weight-module]],
[[prop-qg8-categorification-transports-across-the-hecke-klr-bridge]]).

[C1] Choice is inherited through the quantum highest-weight and global-basis
suppliers; the finite grading and pairing arguments add none
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The intrinsic radical is homogeneous.** For restricted $\lambda$, let $R_\lambda$ be the ungraded cell-form radical in $S(\lambda)$. By [F1] it is the unique maximal proper submodule, and the same is true after scalar extension to the infinite field $K=F(u)$: the Gram kernel extends to $K\otimes_F R_\lambda$ and the quotient remains simple. The same argument also works over an infinite algebraic closure; using $F(u)$ requires no algebraic-closure choice. For $t\in K^\times$ define $s_t(a)=t^ja$ on $B_j$ and $g_t(v)=t^kv$ on $S(\lambda)_k$. The grading gives $g_t(av)=s_t(a)g_t(v)$, so $g_t$ takes submodules to submodules and preserves the unique maximal one. If $v=\sum_{k\in E}v_k$ belongs to this radical, all $\sum_k t^kv_k$ do. The distinct Laurent monomials $t^k$ are linearly independent as functions on the infinite field: multiply a vanishing relation by a large power of $t$ and use the root bound for a polynomial. Thus one can select $|E|$ values of $t$ with invertible evaluation matrix, and solve for each $v_k$ in the radical. It is homogeneous over $K$, hence over $F$, since $v_k\otimes1\in K\otimes R_\lambda$ implies $v_k\in R_\lambda$. Therefore the quotient $\dot D(\lambda)=S(\lambda)/R_\lambda$ has its actual quotient grading and is irreducible even after forgetting that grading. No homogeneity or degree of the cellular form has been assumed. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 **Categorical duality transports to the adjoint upper bar in both branches.** The projective $Be(\mathbf i)$ is $\#$-self-dual: evaluation sends $\operatorname{HOM}_B(Be(\mathbf i),B)$ to $e(\mathbf i)B$, and twisting by the generator-fixing $\psi$ gives $Be(\mathbf i)$ with no shift. Under [F7] its image is a word $F_{i_d}\cdots F_{i_1}v_{\Lambda_0}$, which lower bar fixes since it fixes the vacuum and every $F_i$. These words span each rational weight space. Thus the semilinear projective duality transported by $\phi$ equals lower bar over $\mathbb Q(q)$, and hence on the integral lattice as well; ordinary words need not generate that lattice integrally. Evaluation of a tensor functional gives $D(P^\psi\otimes_BM)=\operatorname{HOM}_B(P,D_\psi M)$, so $\overline{T(P,M)}=h(P,D_\psi M)=T(P^\#,D_\psi M)$. Consequently $\Psi(D_\psi M)(x)=\overline{\Psi(M)(\overline{x})}$, the adjoint upper bar on the restricted dual. This uses only [F6, F7], so holds in (CP) as well as (C0), without identifying positive-characteristic simples with a global basis. [F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 **Completeness of the graded list and uniqueness of shifts.** Let $M$ be any finite-dimensional graded simple $B$-module. Its underlying module has a simple submodule, which is isomorphic to the underlying $\dot D(\lambda)$ for some restricted $\lambda$ by [F1]. An ungraded embedding $f:\dot D(\lambda)\to M$ decomposes into finitely many homogeneous maps $f_r$: for homogeneous $a,v$, comparing degree components in $f(av)=af(v)$ gives $f_r(av)=af_r(v)$. A nonzero $f_r$ has zero kernel since its source is ungraded simple, and its image is a nonzero graded submodule, hence all of $M$. It is therefore a graded isomorphism from the suitable shift of $\dot D(\lambda)$. The same decomposition applied to an ungraded isomorphism between two graded lifts proves that they differ by a shift. Distinct labels cannot become isomorphic by [F1]; a nonzero finite-dimensional graded vector space cannot equal a nonzero shift of itself because its finite degree support would have to be invariant under a nonzero translation. Thus the list in (1) is complete and pairwise distinct. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **The standard-class bar difference is strictly lower.** By [F3], for restricted $\lambda$ the upper expansion is $\operatorname{Std}_\lambda=G^*(\lambda)+\sum_{\nu\lhd\lambda}d_{(\nu,\lambda)}G^*(\nu)$. Upper bar fixes every $G^*(\nu)$ and reverses coefficients, so its difference from $\operatorname{Std}_\lambda$ is a combination of strictly smaller upper vectors. The finite dominance-unitriangular restricted matrix has a triangular inverse over $A$; hence each smaller upper vector is itself a combination of restricted $\operatorname{Std}_\eta$ with $\eta\unlhd\nu\lhd\lambda$. Applying [F3] and step 1.2 gives $[S(\lambda)^\circledast]-[S(\lambda)]\in\sum_{\eta\lhd\lambda}A[S(\eta)]$. This is a statement in the upper integral dual lattice, not in an asserted self-dual lower lattice. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **The actual graded triangular expansion.** A finite graded composition series exists by repeatedly taking a proper graded submodule of maximal dimension. By step 2.1 its factors, after forgetting grading, are the absolutely simple heads of [F1]. Their ungraded multiplicities and dominance support therefore give $[S(\mu)]=\sum_{\lambda\unlhd\mu}c_{\lambda\mu}(q)[\dot D(\lambda)]$. If $\mu$ is unrestricted, every such restricted $\lambda$ is strictly smaller. If $\mu$ is restricted, the actual quotient map in step 1.1 has degree zero and supplies $\dot D(\mu)$ once; ungraded diagonal multiplicity $1$ in [F1] excludes all further shifts of that label, so $c_{\mu\mu}=1$. This proves every clause of (2), without extracting labels or grading shifts from a Grothendieck-group rank count. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **The intrinsic head has zero duality shift.** By [F6] the orbit of $\dot D(\lambda)$ contains a $D_\psi$-self-dual representative $L$. Write $\dot D(\lambda)\cong L\langle r\rangle$, so $\dot D(\lambda)^\circledast\cong\dot D(\lambda)\langle-2r\rangle$; denote this integer shift by $m$. This uses the separately proved normalization supplier, not an inference about a homogeneous cell form or its half-degree. Applying exact duality to the expansion in step 3.1 preserves every smaller label's orbit by the same [F6]. Thus the coefficient of $[\dot D(\lambda)]$ in $[S(\lambda)^\circledast]-[S(\lambda)]$ is $q^m-1$, while step 2.2 and the triangular expansions in step 3.1 make it zero. The simple shift-orbit classes are a free $A$-basis (graded Jordan--Hölder, step 2.1), so $q^m=1$ in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$, forcing $m=0$. This proves the asserted self-duality in both branches and finishes (1). [F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

5.1 **The (C0) crystal label is the intrinsic head label.** In (C0), [F4] gives $[S(\mu)]=\sum_{\lambda\unlhd\mu}d_{(\lambda,\mu)}[D(\lambda)]$ with diagonal $1$. Both the intrinsic heads of step 4.1 and the $D(\lambda)$ are normalized self-dual representatives of the same simple orbits, so their bases differ by a permutation, with no shifts. Induct through a finite linear extension of dominance: after the strictly smaller labels have been identified, subtract their terms from the two expansions of $S(\lambda)$. The remaining leading class is both $[\dot D(\lambda)]$ and $[D(\lambda)]$, proving equality and hence graded isomorphism. This establishes only the (C0) crystal-label clause of (3). [F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 **The ordinary dictionary and Choice.** Independently, the intrinsic nondegenerate form on the ungraded cell head gives its raw-Murphy-star duality by $v\mapsto\langle v,-\rangle$. The Laurent-unit form identity of [F5] identifies the cell radicals and quotients, including the zero case, after every stated field specialization. Through the right-to-left star conversion and involutive sign pullback this gives the ungraded identification $\dot D(\lambda)\cong(D_{\rm DJ}^{\lambda'})^\theta$ in both branches, with the reflected ordinary residue content described in the Statement. This raw cellular-star comparison is separate from the transported $\psi$ duality used in the categorical duality argument; no equality of those anti-involutions has been inferred. The (CP) crystal-label assertion remains unasserted. All new grading and interpolation arguments are finite; Choice is precisely inherited through [C1]. [F5, F6, C1, step 5.1] ∎
